raw_plan.interpretation: A cold acquisition email to independent repair shop owners who are considering whether customers should be able to inspect repair stages. The email should introduce the documented mechanism and invite them to inspect a sample, without implying an existing system, failed process, or planned software project.
raw_plan.reader: Independent repair shop owners considering how customers can inspect repair stages.
raw_plan.reader_segment: Independent repair shop owners considering how customers can inspect repair stages.
raw_plan.reader_scope: Write only to owners evaluating customer visibility into repair stages; do not assume a current tool, workflow problem, implementation plan, or prior software project.
raw_plan.promise: Repairboard gives a shop a shared view of each repair's current stage and a read-only link it can share with a customer; the owner can inspect a sample before deciding whether the approach merits further evaluation.
raw_plan.orientation: Repairboard is a shared repair-status board that can give customers a read-only view of repair stages.
raw_plan.arc: Move a cold reader from not knowing what Repairboard is to being able to judge its core customer-facing status-board mechanism from a sample.
raw_plan.sequence_rationale: One email is sufficient because the requested first step is narrow and low-commitment. It introduces the mechanism, addresses the supported concern about customer editing, and sends the reader to the fixed sample destination. No status quo or failure is asserted because the available material establishes neither.

emails.selection_reason: This proposition directly matches the reader's stated consideration—how customers might inspect repair stages—and offers a concrete evaluation without presuming a software initiative.
emails.job: Earn a visit to the sample board so the owner can decide whether Repairboard's way of presenting repair stages is relevant to their shop.
emails.single_idea: Repairboard displays each repair's current stage on a shared board and lets a shop share a read-only status link with its customer; the reader can judge the basic approach by viewing a sample.
emails.felt_need: I want to see what giving customers visibility into repair stages could look like.
emails.mechanism: Repairboard places each repair's current stage on a shared board, and the shop can provide a customer with a read-only status link.
emails.belief_shift: Before: Repairboard is an unfamiliar product that may imply a larger software undertaking. After: it is a specific shared-board mechanism the owner can inspect through a sample before considering anything further.
must_not_say: Do not claim that shops currently field excessive status calls or use any particular manual process.
Do not imply the reader has an installed system, a failed software project, or an active implementation plan.
Do not promise time savings, fewer calls, higher customer satisfaction, or any other customer outcome.
Do not claim customer adoption, testimonials, popularity, novelty, or superiority over alternatives.
Do not state or imply pricing, a free plan, setup effort, integrations, security, support, or implementation requirements.
Do not describe the sample visit as a trial, demo, consultation, or commitment.
emails.objection: Would a customer-facing link allow the customer to change the repair status? The documented link is read-only.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether this presentation of repair stages is relevant enough to evaluate further for the shop.
emails.next_step_value: See how Repairboard displays current repair stages on a sample shared board.
emails.next_step_limit: The sample does not establish how Repairboard would fit the shop's existing workflow or what setup would require.
emails.subject_strategy: Name the concrete customer-view concept or sample-board evaluation without manufacturing urgency, pain, or a software-project premise.

raw_plan.voice_notes: Use plain, direct language from one person to one person. Keep the opening short and avoid marketing superlatives.
